title: MVP (Model-View-Presenter) Pattern
oneLiner: Makes the View completely passive, moving all presentation logic into a Presenter that's fully testable without any UI framework.

hero.name: The Go-Between
hero.catchphrase: The view doesn't think. I think for it, and I'm the one you test.
hero.power: Mediates entirely between a dumb, passive View and the Model, so all presentation logic can be unit tested without touching the UI.
hero.weakness: The View interface and Presenter can grow chatty with lots of small pass-through methods, feeling like boilerplate for simple screens.
hero.origin: The Go-Between appeared after a mobile app's login screen logic was impossible to unit test because it was baked directly into the Android Activity class, requiring a full emulator just to test a validation rule.

story.problem: Login validation logic ("email must contain @", "password must be 8+ characters") lives directly inside the Android Activity class. Testing it requires spinning up a full emulator, just to check a string.
story.solution: The Go-Between extracts a `LoginPresenter` that holds all the validation and coordination logic. The Activity becomes a passive `LoginView` that just displays what the Presenter tells it to.
story.result: LoginPresenter's logic is now tested with plain unit tests — no emulator, no UI framework, milliseconds instead of minutes.

before: Presentation logic lives inside the UI framework's own classes
Testing logic requires running the full UI (emulator, browser)
The View makes its own decisions about what to display
after: Presentation logic lives in a plain, framework-free Presenter class
Testing logic requires only a unit test, no UI framework
The View is passive — it only displays what the Presenter tells it

panels.label: The Problem
panels.caption: A test suite takes 4 minutes to check one password-validation rule, because it has to boot a full emulator.
panels.speaker: Developer
panels.dialogue: Our CI pipeline spends four minutes booting an emulator just to test that passwords need eight characters. This can't be right.

panels.label: The Hero Arrives
panels.caption: The Go-Between steps in between the Activity and the validation logic, taking on all the thinking.
panels.speaker: The Go-Between
panels.dialogue: Your View shouldn't think for itself. Let me hold the logic — the View just displays whatever I decide.

panels.label: Pattern Power
panels.caption: LoginPresenter.onLoginClicked() validates and calls view.showError() or view.navigateToHome(). The View has no logic of its own.
panels.speaker: The Go-Between
panels.dialogue: I hold every decision. The View just implements simple methods like showError() — it never decides anything on its own.

panels.label: The Result
panels.caption: The same validation test now runs in 4 milliseconds, no emulator involved.
panels.speaker: Developer
panels.dialogue: Four minutes down to four milliseconds. The logic is fully testable now, completely separate from the UI framework.

useWhen: You need presentation logic to be unit testable without booting a UI framework, browser, or emulator.
You're building on a UI framework (older Android, WinForms, legacy desktop UIs) where the 'View' classes are heavy and hard to test directly.
You want a clean, explicit contract (an interface) between presentation logic and the actual UI rendering.
avoidWhen: Your UI framework already supports rich, declarative data binding — MVVM often fits better and needs less boilerplate.
The screen is simple enough that a Presenter's ceremony (interface, pass-through methods) outweighs the testing benefit.
The team has no real need to unit test presentation logic in isolation.
commonMistakes: Letting the View make its own decisions (e.g. conditionally hiding an element based on data) instead of being told exactly what to do by the Presenter.
Creating an overly chatty View interface with dozens of tiny methods, adding boilerplate without meaningfully improving testability.
Putting business logic (not just presentation logic) into the Presenter, blurring the line between Model and Presenter responsibilities.
Confusing MVP with MVC — MVP's View is deliberately passive and fully mediated; classic MVC's View can interact more directly with the Model.
explanation.realWorldExample: Android's traditional MVP architecture (before Jetpack's ViewModel/Compose), and legacy WinForms/WPF apps using MVP for testable presentation logic, are classic real-world MVP implementations.

conversation.speaker: Mentor
conversation.message: How passive does the View really need to be?

conversation.speaker: The Go-Between
conversation.message: Completely. The View should have almost no logic — no if-statements about what to show. It just implements simple methods like showError() and navigateToHome(), and I decide when to call them.

conversation.speaker: Mentor
conversation.message: When should I reach for MVVM instead of you?

conversation.speaker: The Go-Between
conversation.message: When your framework supports real data binding. MVVM lets the View bind directly to observable state — no explicit interface, no manual method calls. I'm the right tool when that binding machinery isn't available.

codeBattle.scenario: Your legacy WinForms desktop app has form-validation and business-flow logic baked directly into code-behind files, making it impossible to unit test without launching the actual application window.
codeBattle.question: Which hero should you call?
codeBattle.explanation: The Go-Between extracts the logic into a testable Presenter behind a simple View interface, which fits WinForms' non-declarative-binding UI model well.

quiz.question: What is the defining characteristic of the View in MVP?
options: It's passive — it has no logic of its own and only displays what the Presenter tells it to
It directly queries the database itself
It contains all the business logic
It communicates only with other Views, never the Presenter
quiz.answer: It's passive — it has no logic of its own and only displays what the Presenter tells it to
quiz.explanation: This deliberate passivity is exactly what makes the Presenter's logic fully testable in isolation.

quiz.question: What's the main testability benefit of MVP?
options: Presenter logic can be unit tested with a fake View, without any real UI framework
It eliminates the need for any tests
It makes UI tests run inside a real browser automatically
It requires a live database connection for every test
quiz.answer: Presenter logic can be unit tested with a fake View, without any real UI framework
quiz.explanation: Because the View is just an interface, a lightweight fake/mock can stand in during Presenter tests.

quiz.question: How does MVP differ from classic MVC?
options: MVP's View is deliberately passive and fully mediated by the Presenter; classic MVC's View can interact more directly with the Model
They are identical patterns with different names
MVC requires a Presenter; MVP does not
MVP can only be used on mobile platforms
quiz.answer: MVP's View is deliberately passive and fully mediated by the Presenter; classic MVC's View can interact more directly with the Model
quiz.explanation: The degree of View passivity is the key structural difference between the two related patterns.

quiz.question: When might MVVM be preferable to MVP?
options: When the UI framework supports rich, declarative data binding, reducing manual pass-through code
When the team wants to avoid testing presentation logic entirely
When there's no need to separate the View from logic
When the application has no UI at all
quiz.answer: When the UI framework supports rich, declarative data binding, reducing manual pass-through code
quiz.explanation: MVVM's binding mechanism can eliminate much of the boilerplate that MVP's explicit View interface requires.
